data.title: Trump says he told Zacharia to 'reconsider' press secretary role
data.description:
President Trump told reporters on Friday that he told Katie Zacharia that she should” reconsider” her role as White House press secretary after her rocky start to the job this week. 

“I said, ‘honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,'” Trump told reporters, referring to a conversation he said he had with Zacharia earlier. 

“I said, ‘you think about it, but I would reconsider,'” he continued. 

Trump told reporters the decision is ultimately up to Zacharia, but that the decision was up to her. When asked how much time he will give her, Trump said he will talk to her when he gets back. The president is heading to Georgia for a rally then to Florida for much of the weekend.

Trump said he wants Zacharia “to be happy” and said the news media has treated unfairly.

DEVELOPING

data.title: Can voters learn to stop worrying and love Big AI?
data.description:
Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), who told me he uses chatbots “all the time,” appears confident Republicans are misplaying their hand with the AI industry. Americans have reason to feel that the AI revolution is “something that is happening to them, not for them,” Schiff told me. “AI industry leaders themselves have been clear about the need for federal safeguards. Unenforceable voluntary commitments and self-regulation will not cut it.”

A few Tuesdays earlier, the mood at the White House had been considerably more celebratory. President Trump hosted a who’s who of tech titans in Washington, D.C., for the signing of an AI safety pact. (Sorry, superintelligence or “SI.”) The meeting yielded what Trump called a “morally binding” agreement to develop AI for the common good. The means of securing this happy outcome is to entrust the industry to “self-police” and “self-regulate” rather than face federal regulation.

Will Americans accept an industry’s freedom to remake their lives as the price of national greatness? Trump has made that bet on his party’s behalf — a stark contrast, at least in rhetoric, to what he said back in June. Asked about Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-Vt.) proposal for public ownership of AI, he said, “There’s something very interesting about it, where it almost becomes a partnership with the American public,” according to the Associated Press. Trump also told reporters that his voters and Sanders’s “aren’t that far apart” on economics. If that much is true, then — as some Republican candidates are now discovering — the promise of American supremacy should offer limited comfort to Americans who suspect they’ll have little say in the terms of their own future.

Advocates of AI deregulation have found a receptive audience in Washington, with Republican candidates adopting their refrain: let Big AI move fast and break things, lest China get there first. “Under [the] Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country because in two years, China is going to be so far ahead, we’re going to be in so much trouble,” said Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) in a Senate debate days ago after her Democratic opponent dubbed her “Data Center Darline.”

While Democrats are clearly fractured over AI — with many, including Schiff, opposed to such lengthy moratoriums — some Republicans facing tough elections seem to doubt the marching orders from Trump’s White House will help them win. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for governor in Wisconsin who in January called data centers an “exciting new technology” and voted in Congress to speed up their permitting, released a James Fishback-style “aura farming” edit video immediately following the primary election distinguishing himself from his opponent “Data Center David Crowley.” In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers backed a yearlong moratorium on data center construction two weeks after affordability champion Abdul El-Sayed became the Democratic nominee, while continuing to attack El-Sayed’s support for public ownership of AI.

There is a clear mismatch between voters’ misgivings on the ground and the way Trump wants to get around the problem: that if he can get Americans excited enough about “Super Intelligence,” his party’s political liabilities will take care of themselves. “These Republicans who are responding to public sentiment and doing something about AI are the ones in competitive races. They’re not getting orders from the top,” Saikat Chakrabarti, the progressive tech multimillionaire and former Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) chief of staff, told me.

Democrats’ quarrels may yet prove an advantage: a party still arguing about AI gives its candidates, especially progressives who decline Big AI’s super PAC money, latitude to articulate the public’s misgivings. “The Schiff wing is saying we should do some regulation because I know we have to say we have to do some regulation,” Chakrabarti continued. “I think the Bernie wing is taking it the most seriously, but even that answer right now is let’s pause and figure it out. Whoever has the answer to that next crisis is going to win 90 percent of the country in the next election.”

Schiff, for his part, told me he is working on a legislative proposal “[rethinking] what unemployment compensation will look like” and other things, to be introduced in the coming months. There is, at least, some figuring out underway.

Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, whom the Democratic campaign of James Talarico has shelled with ads about his ambiguous support for data centers, sounds less than delighted. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign,” he lamented in private, “like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming — you know — from DC. I don’t control the message or what we’re doing.”

Paxton, like Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, now backs tighter restrictions on data center development after previously taking a more supportive stance. Republicans are making a considerable wager that the prospect of winning the AI arms race will reconcile Americans to whatever the industry has planned for them. They’re increasingly finding themselves drawn into the same arguments now consuming Democrats, whatever the president would prefer.

William Liang is a writer living in San Francisco. He volunteers for Connie Chan’s congressional campaign in California’s 11th District.

data.title: Musk settles election lottery lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaways
data.description:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk agreed to settle two lawsuits over his $1 million check handouts to battleground voters in the 2024 election, according to court filings published Thursday.

The suits, filed in the Western District of Texas, accused the Tesla and SpaceX CEO of defrauding voters when his political action committee (PAC), America PAC, offered a $1 million giveaway to swing state voters every day leading up to the 2024 general election.

Musk first made the pledge in October 2024 in Pennsylvania, and eventually made similar promises in Michigan, Nevada, Arizona, Georgia, Wisconsin and North Carolina.

“The only thing we ask for the million dollars is that you be a spokesperson for the petition,” Musk told a recipient he handpicked from the audience at the time.

The lawsuits argued that voters were misled when they signed the petition and were told recipients would be chosen at “random” as in a lottery. Musk told a Philadelphia judge that winners were not chosen by random but chosen to be paid “spokespeople for the group.”

The tech mogul was ordered to testify under oath in June but had not yet testified before the settlements were reached. The details of the settlement were not included in public filings, and The Hill reached out to the plaintiffs’ and Musk’s legal teams for more information.

In Wisconsin, Musk made a different pledge for $1 million check handouts to voters during the state’s Supreme Court election last year.

Musk initially announced in March 2025 that he would speak in Wisconsin, with entrance limited to those who had voted in the state’s Supreme Court election. He said on the social platform X he would “personally hand over two checks for a million dollars each in appreciation for you taking the time to vote.”

About 12 hours later, his post was deleted and replaced with another, clarifying entrance was limited to those who signed the petition against “activist judges.” Musk said the money would be given to “spokesmen” for the petition, and he went to hand out two checks during a campaign rally in Wisconsin.

La Crosse County, Wisc. District Attorney Tim Gruenke (D) announced in August his office declined to press charges over the handouts, arguing that in the end, “nobody was paid anything of value for voting or promising to vote.”

Despite Musk’s efforts, the conservative candidate he backed, Brad Schimel, lost to Democratic-backed Susan Crawford, keeping the high court’s liberal majority.

While Musk has not made similar pledges this election cycle, the SpaceX CEO is shaping up to be the largest known donor of the 2026 midterms for Republicans.

data.title: Brown, Acton both up 6 points in Ohio races: poll
data.description:
A new poll of the Ohio Senate and gubernatorial races shows Democrats ahead in both contests.

In the Senate race, a Bowling Green State University (BGSU) poll found former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) ahead of Sen. Jon Husted (R) by six points, 48 percent to 42 percent, among likely voters. When BGSU surveyed the race in September, Brown had just a three-point lead.

Ohio voters are evenly split 48 to 48 on who they think will win, regardless of who they support. That is narrower from September, when more thought Husted would win.

In the governor’s race, Democrat Amy Acton leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy also by six points, 50 percent to 44 percent. In BGSU’s September poll, Acton had a three-point lead. Most still think Ramaswamy is likely to win in the end, 55 to 43, though that is a closer margin than in BGSU’s September poll.

Ohio was long a battleground state but has moved towards Republicans in the last decade, starting with President Trump’s win in 2016. Former Vice President Harris lost Ohio by 11 points in 2024, and Brown lost his Senate seat that year by 3.5 points.

BGSU notes in its survey that Democrats in Ohio are more motivated to vote than Republicans, 59 percent to 41 percent, a narrower edge than in BGSU’s September poll.

BGSU Political Science Professor Robert Alexander said while Democrats may be ahead now, they should not celebrate just yet.

“While this will be welcome news to Democrats, a blue wave in Ohio is far from a sure thing,” Alexander said. “Republicans have closed well in recent statewide elections, and I would be surprised if these races did not end up within the margin of error in either direction.”

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, agrees that the Ohio race is close, giving Brown just a 53 percent shot at flipping the seat.

The battleground Senate races have been inundated with political ads throughout the cycle, and Ohio voters expressed fatigue in the BGSU poll.

Just 6 percent of likely Ohio voters want to see more political ads before Election Day, while 60 percent say the ads are largely negative, which has caused them to tune out campaign ads altogether.

“Ohio voters remain deeply engaged in this election, but they are also telling us that the nonstop barrage of political advertising has become overwhelming,” Alexander said. 

The BGSU poll, conducted in partnership with YouGov, was a web-based survey of 1,000 likely Ohio voters fielded from Sept. 29-Oct. 9. The margin of error is +/- 3.95 points.

data.title: AI safety group pushes for tighter export controls, limits on 'vastly superhuman AI'
data.description:
A conservative AI safety group is calling for the U.S. to implement tighter restrictions on advanced chip sales to China and limit the development of “vastly superhuman AI” as part of a new framework for AI policy.

Humans First, chaired by former Tea Party leader Amy Kremer, laid out what it described as an “America First” policy framework.

“AI will supercharge our nation’s economy, improve our quality of life, and ensure we dominate around the world,” it wrote. “But policy must always be focused on helping hardworking Americans and putting Humans First.”

The group is arguing for stricter export controls on high-end chips and other AI technologies, mandatory testing of models for extreme risks, mandatory public reporting of major AI incidents, developer liability for “reckless design” and a “red line” on self-improving AI.

It also called for an end to any federal use of Flock cameras and warrantless searches of private data, in addition to urging a halt in H-1B visa approvals and opposing federal preemption of state AI laws.

Humans First, which was initially created to organize across party lines, shifted its focus to conservative activists in April when it tapped Kremer to serve as chair.

The group has been a vocal critic of the data center buildout in recent months, leading a day of nationwide demonstrations in July and staging a cross-country bus tour opposing the AI infrastructure that wrapped up earlier this month.

The group’s AI framework stands in contrast to the more hands-off approach currently championed by President Trump, who has argued stricter regulations could hamper the U.S.’s ability to compete with China.

Trump gathered major AI leaders at the White House late last month, where they signed onto a series of voluntary commitments to place internal controls on their models and allow for external auditing.

data.title: Judge tosses Trump administration lawsuit over NYC 'sanctuary' laws
data.description:
A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit brought by the Trump administration to block New York City laws that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, saying the government lacked a valid basis to sue.

U.S. District ​Judge Ramon Reyes in Brooklyn said the Trump administration cannot challenge a ⁠city law that restricts police from detaining immigrants at ​the request of federal immigration authorities, Reuters reported Thursday.  

“The federal government came to court seeking to force New York City to turn its public servants into deportation agents and divert our resources toward carrying out ICE’s cruel agenda,” said New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a written statement following the ruling. “Today, they lost.”

Last year in July, the Trump administration filed the lawsuit in a Federal District Court in Brooklyn claiming that the city’s policies violate the supremacy clause of the Constitution, which gives federal laws precedence over state laws, The New York Times reported. Reyes rejected those arguments, declaring the federal government cannot force local ​governments to ⁠assist with immigration enforcement, the Reuters report said.

“Our local laws make New York City safer. They allow us to focus our resources on protecting and serving our communities and ensuring that every New Yorker can turn to their City government without fear that asking for help will make them a target for deportation,” the mayor said in his statement.

In the ruling, the judge also supported the validity of the city laws restricting local authorities from sharing release dates, ​whereabouts or other custody information about immigrants as federal law does not require state and local ‌governments ⁠to share that information, according to the Reuters report.

The ruling comes a week after a U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in New York City in the Bronx’s Marble Hill neighborhood. The Department of Homeland Security said the 28-year-old man entered the country illegally and had a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession.

Following the incident, Mamdani in a social media post called it “an incredibly serious situation.”

“I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city,” he wrote. “I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities.”

data.title: Main Trump legal fund $1.9M in debt
data.description:
President Trump’s primary legal fund is more than $1.9 million in debt, according to its latest filing with the Federal Election Commission (FEC).

Save America PAC, which Trump formed after he lost the 2020 presidential election, spent more than $5.4 million in the third quarter and had spent more than $14 million from the start of the year through September, per its quarterly filing to the FEC.

At the start of the year, the president had nearly $1.2 million on hand. The fund had roughly $673,000 as of the end of June. But as of the end of the third quarter, it had less than $33,000.

The PAC also owes more than $1.9 million to legal firms and received roughly $4.7 million in transfers from Never Surrender PAC, another Trump-affiliated group, from July through September.

The Hill has reached out to a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., another super PAC that supports the president.

Save America lists all the debts it holds as legal consulting or legal fees and expenses. They range from about $239,000 owed to Brito PLLC — whose founder, Alejandro Brito, represented the president in multiple lawsuits he filed against ABC News, BBC and other media outlets. 

In the defamation suit against ABC, the company agreed to settle by providing $15 million towards Trump’s future presidential library. 

Save America also owes about $760,000 to Sullivan & Cromwell LLP, which is representing Trump in his appeal of a New York jury’s 2024 ruling convicting him on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records.

Dhillon Law Group, which Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon founded in 2006, is owed $34,000. Dhillon, who runs the Justice Department’s (DOJ) Civil Rights Division, departed the firm when she officially joined the administration last year.

The Hill also reached out to the DOJ.

The fund’s debts decreased in the third quarter, as the PAC reported owing more than $3.7 million at the end of the second quarter. The amount the organization owes to Brito’s firm and Sullivan & Cromwell rose from nearly $169,000 and roughly $335,600 as of the end of quarter two, respectively, according to the FEC.

Its obligations to Dhillon Law Group, meanwhile, decreased from roughly $96,500 as of the end of the second quarter.

data.title: Zacharia says Trump didn't ask whether she passed bar exam
data.description:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia weighed in on the controversy surrounding her law career Friday, saying President Trump did not ask questions about whether she passed the bar exam when she was appointed to her role.

When asked by Fox News about reporting that she did not pass the test, Zacharia said, “Those questions weren’t asked.”

“I’m being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel,” she told the “Fox & Friends” hosts. “The reason that I was hired was to represent the president in the press.”

Zacharia started making headlines as soon as she stepped in to her new role, particularly about her claims of being a lawyer as reports surfaced about her not being licensed to practice law in any U.S. state. A watchdog group called the Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California asking for an investigation into her claim.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the group’s executive director, said in a statement.

Reporters also pressed her on where she passed the exam.

The press secretary responded, “When I moved to China.”

Zacharia later said she misheard the question.

“I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she told The New York Times on Wednesday. The president also called her “an attorney” in his Truth Social post announcing her appointment as his spokesperson.

The Wall Street Journal also reported that Zacharia took the California bar exam after she received her law degree from Pepperdine University, but she did not pass. She said Thursday that the results of the test are “somewhat inconsequential.”

Zacharia was previously a communications adviser for Trump Media and Technology Group, the company behind the president’s Truth Social platform, and also served at one time as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security.

She started her new role earlier this week, holding a 14-minute press briefing Tuesday morning. During the brief exchange with reporters, she took three questions and dropped the news about the resignation of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.

Zacharia was appointed to fill the gap left by Karoline Leavitt, who departed the administration earlier this year.

data.title: Are dark days ahead for Republicans after the midterm elections?
data.description:
You have to hand it to President Trump. He has managed to offend Democrats, alienate independents, and now, just for good measure, turn off Republicans, too.

This is not exactly a brilliant political strategy with the midterm elections just a few weeks away.

As a headline in the New York Times put it: “Signs are emerging that dispirited Republican voters may stay home in November.”

Apparently, even some Republicans have had enough. They’re tired of the chaos, tired of the constant feuding, tired of the daily drama. In a word — make that two words — they’re tired of Trump.

The Times quotes a former Republican member of the Michigan House of Representatives who put it this way: “People are tired. The whole divider-in-chief thing, it’s gotten to the point where it’s just exhausting.”

And it’s a safe bet that he’s not alone.

So what is Trump’s solution? He is telling Republicans to vote as if he were on the ballot. Careful what you wish for. Some Republicans may take his advice — and stay home.

That’s not exactly what Trump had in mind, but then again, nobody has ever accused him of underestimating his own popularity. Trump has always been his own biggest fan. You get the impression that he thinks that because he’s in love with himself, everybody else should be too.

We’ll know soon enough whether he can persuade disillusioned Republicans to show up on Election Day. His pitch is simple: Vote Republican or you’ll regret it. Because if Democrats take control of Congress, he warns, dark days are ahead.

Maybe. But here’s something we can say with considerably more confidence: If Democrats take the House — and possibly the Senate — dark days really will be ahead. This is especially so for Trump and for Republicans, who will suddenly discover what life is like when the other team gets to call the plays.

So what can the president expect if his party winds up on the outside looking in? Let’s start with impeachment. The smarter Democrats may recognize that impeaching Trump for a third time would be a political mistake. Even Americans who can’t stand Trump may have little appetite for another impeachment circus.

But the hard left won’t be interested in political wisdom. They will want to publicly humiliate Trump at any cost. And there’s a decent chance that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), if he becomes speaker, will go wobbly. He will discover that standing up to his party’s loudest voices is harder than giving in to them.

As for high crimes and misdemeanors, Democrats will undoubtedly find something that fits their definition. Take your pick: deportations, presidential pardons, the demolition of the White House East Wing, the war in Iran.

And why stop with Trump himself? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and assorted other Trump loyalists could find themselves in the congressional crosshairs.

Then come the investigations. Lots and lots of investigations.

The Trump family business. Jeffrey Epstein. Tariffs. The White House ballroom. The president’s attacks on his critics in the news media. Taxpayer-funded advertisements that just happen to make Trump look wonderful.

Democrats may even try to subpoena the president himself. Good luck with that. He’ll tell them what they can do with their subpoena before he even thinks about going to Capitol Hill to answer questions thrown at him by Democrats who loathe everything about him.

But they might have better luck dragging people around him before congressional committees, people like his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, who knows the kind of stuff Democrats would love to hear from her — while she’s under oath. Another long shot, bordering on no way she would talk. But Democrats won’t care — anything to make Team Trump miserable.

So, get ready for hearings, subpoenas, accusations, counteraccusations and enough political theater to keep cable news in business for another decade.

Of course, none of this is inevitable. Polls have been wrong before. They could be wrong again. But I wouldn’t bet on it.

Too many polls are telling us the same thing: Trump is about as popular — maybe even a little less popular — than the flu. And since midterm elections are essentially a report card on the president, Republicans have good reason to worry —especially when the president is determined to make the election all about himself.

And if the results are as bad as Republicans fear, we won’t have to wait long for the postmortem. It’ll probably begin about 10 seconds after the polls close.

Trump will blame the fake news media. He’ll blame rigged elections. He’ll blame RINOs, disloyal Republicans, lousy candidates and anybody else who happens to be within shouting distance.

But there’s one thing we can count on: Whatever happens on Election Day, Trump will find somebody to blame. And we all know who it won’t be.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page.

data.title: ICE officers 'did not identify themselves' ahead of Bronx shooting: Lawyers
data.description:
Lawyers for the man shot by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New York City say the officers involved “did not identify themselves” before they opened fire on him, according to recent court filings. 

On Oct. 8, Oscar Belgal was picking up his 5-year-old son before he was stopped by ICE officers who also did not “show any documents or otherwise communicate with [Belgal] in any substantive way,” Legal Aid Society, a group representing Belgal, described.

The group continued in the 58-page document filed Wednesday that “without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat.”

“One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed. Believing that his dad had been fatally shot, his son screamed hysterically that  the masked men had killed his father,” the filing states. 

The incident, which was captured on ICE officer body cameras, resulted in Belgal being taken to an area hospital, while his child remains unharmed and with a family member, according to New York Police Department (NYPD) Commissioner Jessica Tisch. The body camera footage has not been released.

Legal Aid attorneys serving as counsel for Belgal, Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams, said in a press release that their client’s ICE detention was “unlawful from its inception.”

 “With a bullet still lodged in his neck and his serious medical needs unmet, every additional day in custody puts him at further risk. The Court must intervene and order his immediate release,” McAninch and Williams stated. 

In the hours following the shooting, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he called President Trump and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin to negotiate Belgal’s release from federal custody but was “unsuccessful.”

Mullin detailed the phone call, saying at a press conference that Trump agreed to move Belgal to NYPD’s custody if charges against him were to be prosecuted but, according to Mullin, Mamdani did not agree.

The secretary further accused Belgal of participating in “extensive criminal activity” and stated ICE officers involved in the incident were not aware of Belgal’s son in the backseat. Mullin stated the ICE officers will be put on administrative leave while the department investigates the incident, 

Mamdani has also called for ICE to release the body-camera footage of the incident. The NYPD has already released body-camera footage from its officers of the moments after the shooting.
